intro: The Daodejing and the Zhuangzi are the two great early books of Daoist thought. They speak of the Dao, the Way, and of acting without forcing. They teach with pictures: water, an empty bowl, an uncarved block, a swimmer, a cook and a frog.

In this unit you will learn the big ideas: Dao, wu wei, yin and yang, and de. Then you will read the images the books use to teach them. You will also learn that Daoism is studied as a philosophy and practiced by many people as a religion.
By the end, you can explain each big idea with a passage. You can tell what an image means to its readers. You can compare how Daoist books teach with how the Analects teaches.
bigQuestion: What do the Daodejing and the Zhuangzi teach about the Way, and why do they teach with pictures?

write.prompt: Choose one Daoist idea: wu wei or simplicity. Explain it using two or three passages, such as Daodejing 8, 11 or 37 and Zhuangzi 3 or 19 (Legge's translations, 1891). Tell what each passage says and how readers have understood it.
tips: Name the book and chapter each time.
Say 'the Daodejing says' or 'Daoists teach'; do not state your own belief as fact.
Explain the image before you explain the idea.
Use unit words like wu wei, pu and ziran.

title: Key Teachings of the Dao

chapters.title: The Dao, Wu Wei and Yin-Yang
chapters.bigQuestion: What does it mean to go with the Way instead of forcing things?

story.title: Stop Fighting the Water
story.kicker: A swimmer stops fighting a strong current and floats safely to shore.
paragraphs: Jada was swimming in Lake Michigan on a windy summer day. She had gone out farther than she meant to. When she turned back, the water pulled her sideways along the beach. She kicked hard toward shore. She got nowhere.

Her arms grew tired. Her heart pounded. Then she remembered what the lifeguard had told her class: 'If a current pulls you, don't fight it head-on. Float. Swim across it, along the shore. Then come in.'
Jada rolled onto her back and floated. She breathed slowly. Then she swam sideways, with easy strokes, parallel to the beach. Little by little, the pull let go. She turned and swam in.
On the sand, she sat wrapped in a towel. The lifeguard sat beside her. 'You did it right,' he said. 'Fighting the water wears you out. Working with it gets you home.'
Jada thought about that for a long time. Her grandmother had once shown her an old Chinese book that talked about water, and about acting without forcing. Now she wanted to read it again.
story.think: When have you gotten further by working with something instead of fighting it?

lessons.title: A Way Without a Name
lessons.mainIdea: The Daodejing says the Dao is beyond names; 'Dao,' the Way, is only a word used to point to it.
reading: *Dao* means way, road or path. Confucius used it for the right way to live and govern. The Daodejing uses it for something larger: the source and pattern of everything.
In chapter 25, the Daodejing describes something that existed before heaven and earth. It says: I do not know its name. I call it Dao. If I must describe it, I call it great.
So the book says Dao is not really a name. It is a word to point at something words cannot hold. Readers compare it to a finger pointing at the moon: look at the moon, not the finger.

words.d: the Way; in the Daodejing, the nameless source and pattern of all things
the place something comes from

look.title: Daodejing 25

look.cite: Daodejing, chapter 25, retold simply from James Legge's translation (The Tao Teh King, 1891)
look.prompt: Why does the speaker say he does not know its name?

lessons.title: One, Two, Three, All Things
lessons.mainIdea: Daodejing 42 says the Dao gives rise to one, two, three and all things.
reading: Chapter 42 of the Daodejing has a short, famous line. The Dao gave birth to one. One gave birth to two. Two gave birth to three. Three gave birth to all things.
The chapter does not explain exactly what one, two and three are. Readers have offered many answers. Many say two means yin and yang, which the same chapter goes on to name.
The big idea is that everything comes from the Dao. The Daodejing calls the Dao the mother of all things in chapter 1 and elsewhere. Things arise, grow and return to it.

words.d: where something begins
one reader's explanation of what a text means

look.title: Daodejing 42
look.text: The Dao produced One. One produced Two. Two produced Three. Three produced all things.
look.cite: Daodejing, chapter 42, retold simply from James Legge's translation (1891)
look.prompt: What might 'two' stand for? Why do readers disagree about it?

check.q: In Daodejing 42, what does three produce?
check.why: The chapter says three produced all things.

check.q: What do many readers say 'two' means in chapter 42?
check.why: The same chapter goes on to name yin and yang.

check.q: What is an interpretation?
choices: One reader's explanation of what a text means
check.why: Different readers give different interpretations.

lessons.title: Following What Is Natural
lessons.mainIdea: The Daodejing says the Dao follows ziran, what is 'so of itself,' or natural.
reading: Chapter 25 ends with a chain. People follow the earth. The earth follows heaven. Heaven follows the Dao. And the Dao follows *ziran*. It is one of the book's best-known lines.
Ziran literally means 'so of itself.' It is often translated as natural or spontaneous. It describes things happening by their own nature, without being pushed.
Daoist readers often point to nature as a teacher. Seasons change on their own. Rivers find their way downhill. The Daodejing asks readers to notice this kind of ease.

words.d: 'so of itself'; being natural or spontaneous, happening by its own nature
happening naturally, without being planned or forced

look.title: Nature Without Pushing
look.text: No one pushes the maple trees on your street to turn red in October. No one pulls the rain down to the ground. Birds fly south without a map. The Daodejing calls this kind of happening ziran.
look.prompt: Name one more thing in nature that happens 'so of itself.'

check.q: What does ziran literally mean?
check.why: Ziran means 'so of itself,' natural.

check.q: In chapter 25, what does the Dao follow?
check.why: The chain ends: the Dao follows ziran.

check.q: What does spontaneous mean?
check.why: Spontaneous means happening on its own.

lessons.title: Doing Without Forcing
lessons.mainIdea: Wu wei means acting without forcing; the Daodejing says the Dao does nothing, yet nothing is left undone.
reading: *Wu wei* literally means 'not doing' or 'no action.' But it does not mean being lazy. Scholars explain it as acting without forcing, strain or grabbing.
Chapter 37 says the Dao does nothing, and yet nothing is left undone. Things grow and change without the Dao pushing them. The Daodejing suggests people can act that way too.
Think of an expert. A skilled dancer or basketball player moves smoothly. They do not look like they are forcing it. Many readers use this as a picture of wu wei.

words.d: acting without forcing; effortless action that goes with the way things are
seeming to need no struggle

look.title: Daodejing 37

look.cite: Daodejing, chapter 37, retold simply from James Legge's translation (1891)
look.prompt: How can something 'do nothing' and still get everything done?

check.q: What does wu wei mean, as scholars explain it?
check.why: Wu wei means acting without forcing, not laziness.

check.q: What does chapter 37 say about the Dao?
choices: It does nothing, yet nothing is left undone
check.why: Chapter 37 gives this paradox.

check.q: Which is a good picture of wu wei?
check.why: Skilled, unforced action is a common picture of wu wei.

lessons.title: The Swimmer at the Waterfall
lessons.mainIdea: In a Zhuangzi story, a swimmer survives a huge waterfall by going with the water, not against it.
reading: The Zhuangzi, chapter 19, tells of Confucius at a great waterfall. The water fell so far and so fast that no fish or turtle could swim there. Then he saw a man in the water.
Confucius thought the man was in trouble. He sent students to help. But the man came out, singing, and walked along the bank. Confucius asked how he did it.

The man said he went down with the swirls and came up with the currents. He followed the water's way and did not force his own. Readers see wu wei in this story. Note that the Zhuangzi often places Confucius in its own stories.

words.d: water moving in one direction
a Daoist thinker of about the 300s BCE, and the book of stories named after him

look.title: The Swimmer

look.cite: Zhuangzi, chapter 19, retold simply from James Legge's translation (The Writings of Kwang-ze, 1891)
look.prompt: How is this swimmer like Jada in the opening story?

check.why: He followed the water and did not force his own way.

check.q: Who watches the swimmer in the story?
check.why: The Zhuangzi places Confucius at the waterfall.

lessons.title: Leading Without Forcing
lessons.mainIdea: The Daodejing says the best leaders are barely noticed, so people feel they did the work themselves.
reading: Chapter 17 of the Daodejing ranks leaders. The best leader, it says, is one the people barely know is there. The next best is loved and praised. Worse is one who is feared.
When the best leader's work is done, the chapter says, the people all say: we did this ourselves. The leader has helped without taking over. The leader's help is real, but it stays in the background.
Readers apply this to many kinds of leading. Coaches, teachers and team captains talk about it. They set things up so others can do their best, without forcing them.

words.d: a person who guides a group
not boastful; not trying to be the center of attention

check.q: What does humble mean?
check.why: Humble means not trying to be the center of attention.

sections.title: Yin, Yang, De and Daoist Practice

lessons.title: Yin and Yang
lessons.mainIdea: Yin and yang are paired opposites that need each other; later artists drew them in the taijitu symbol.
reading: *Yin* first meant the shady side of a hill. *Yang* meant the sunny side. Chinese thinkers came to use them for all pairs of opposites: dark and light, cool and warm, rest and motion.
Yin and yang are not good and evil. They need each other and keep changing into each other. Night turns into day, and day into night. Chapter 42 of the Daodejing names them together.
The swirling black-and-white circle is called the *taijitu*. Early forms of this diagram appear in the Song dynasty, about 1,000 years ago. The familiar swirl took shape later still.

words.d: paired opposites, like shade and sun, that need each other and change into each other
the diagram of yin and yang, often drawn as a swirling circle

look.title: Opposites That Need Each Other
look.text: Picture a hill at sunrise. The east side glows in sunlight: yang. The west side lies in shadow: yin. By evening, the sun has moved. Now the west side is bright and the east is shady. The hill is the same. The sides trade places.
look.prompt: How does this picture show that yin and yang change into each other?

choices: The shady side of a hill

check.why: Yin first meant the shady side; yang the sunny side.

check.q: Are yin and yang the same as good and evil?
choices: No, they are paired opposites that need each other
check.why: They are complementary, not good versus evil.

check.q: What is the taijitu?
choices: The diagram of yin and yang
check.why: The taijitu is the yin-yang diagram.

lessons.title: De: Power and Virtue
lessons.mainIdea: De means the power or virtue a thing has when it follows the Dao; the Daodejing says Dao gives life and de nourishes it.
reading: *De* is the second word in the book's title. It is often translated as power, virtue or potency. Legge translated it as virtue. It names the power that the Way gives to things.
In the Daodejing, de is the quiet strength that comes from following the Dao. It is not power over others. It is more like the power a seed has to grow.

Chapter 51 says the Dao gives things life and de nourishes them. Confucius also used the word de, for the good character of a ruler or a junzi. The two traditions share the word but stress different things.

words.d: power or virtue; in the Daodejing, the quiet strength of following the Dao
to feed and help grow

look.title: Daodejing 51

check.why: The Dao gives life and de nourishes.

check.q: How is de like a seed's power?

lessons.title: Philosophy and Religion
lessons.mainIdea: Daoism is studied as a philosophy, and for many people it is also a living religion with temples, priests and rituals.
reading: Some people read the Daodejing and Zhuangzi as philosophy, a way of thinking about life. Others practice Daoism as a religion. Daoist communities have temples, priests, scriptures and festivals.

Tradition says an organized Daoist movement, the Way of the Celestial Masters, began around 142 CE. Daoist believers honor Laozi as a deity. Priests lead rituals, and many Daoists practice meditation and exercises for health.
Scholars used to split Daoism into 'philosophical' and 'religious.' Many now say the line is not so sharp. Daoist priests have read the Daodejing as scripture for many centuries.

words.d: the study of big questions about life, knowledge and right and wrong
a set of beliefs and practices shared by a community, often about the sacred
an early organized Daoist movement, traditionally dated to about 142 CE

chapters.title: Water, the Uncarved Block and Simplicity
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do the Daodejing and the Zhuangzi teach with pictures instead of rules?

story.title: The Knife That Stayed Sharp
story.kicker: A cook's knife stays sharp for nineteen years, and a king asks him how.
paragraphs: In a story from the Zhuangzi, a king named Wenhui watched his cook, Ding, cut up an ox. Ding's hands moved and his shoulders turned. His knife made a soft, even sound, like music. The work looked like a dance.
'Amazing!' said the king. 'How did your skill get this good?' Cook Ding put down his knife. 'What I care about is the Way,' he said. 'It goes beyond skill.'

Ding explained. When he began, he saw only a whole ox in front of him. After three years, he no longer saw the whole ox. Now he felt his way through it. He let his knife follow the natural gaps between the joints.

'A good cook changes his knife every year, because he cuts,' Ding said. 'An ordinary cook changes it every month, because he hacks. I have had this knife for nineteen years. It is still as sharp as the day it was made.'
The king was quiet for a moment. Then he said, 'Wonderful! From the words of Cook Ding, I have learned how to care for life.' People have retold this story for more than 2,000 years.
story.think: What do you think the king learned about life from a cook's knife?

lessons.title: The Highest Good Is Like Water
lessons.mainIdea: Daodejing 8 says the highest good is like water, which helps all things, does not compete and goes to low places.
reading: Water is one of the Daodejing's favorite *images*. An image is a picture in words. Chapter 8 says the highest good is like water. It returns to water again and again.
Why water? The chapter says water benefits all things. It does not fight or compete. It settles in low places that people avoid. The chapter says this makes water close to the Dao.
Readers see a lesson about humility here. Water does not rush to the top. It goes low, and yet everything needs it. Many readers see this as a picture of helping without showing off.

words.d: a picture in words that helps explain an idea
not thinking you are more important than others

look.title: Daodejing 8
look.text: The highest good is like water. Water benefits all things and does not compete. It stays in low places that people dislike. So it is close to the Dao.
look.cite: Daodejing, chapter 8, retold simply from James Legge's translation (The Tao Teh King, 1891)
look.prompt: List three things water does in this chapter. Which one surprises you?

check.q: What does Daodejing 8 say the highest good is like?
check.why: Chapter 8 says the highest good is like water.

check.q: Where does water settle, in chapter 8?
check.why: Water goes to low places that people dislike.

check.q: What is an image, in writing?
check.why: An image is a word-picture that explains an idea.

lessons.title: Soft Overcomes Hard
lessons.mainIdea: The Daodejing says the soft and weak overcome the hard and strong, as water wears away stone.
reading: Chapter 78 says nothing in the world is softer or weaker than water. Yet for attacking what is hard and strong, nothing can beat it. It is a surprising claim about something so gentle.

Chapter 76 adds another picture. When people are alive, their bodies are soft and bendable. When they die, they become stiff. Green plants are soft and supple; dry ones snap. So the book links softness with life.
Readers use these chapters in many ways. Some see advice about patience. Some see a lesson about gentleness in conflict. Martial arts teachers have often quoted the idea too.

words.d: able to bend easily without breaking
to win against or get past something difficult

look.title: Daodejing 78
look.text: Nothing in the world is softer and weaker than water. Yet nothing is better at wearing down what is hard and strong.
look.cite: Daodejing, chapter 78, retold simply from James Legge's translation (1891)
look.prompt: Give one example from nature where something soft wears down something hard.

check.q: What does chapter 78 say is softest and weakest?
check.why: Chapter 78 names water.

check.q: In chapter 76, what is softness linked to?
check.why: Living things are soft and supple; dead things are stiff.

check.q: What does supple mean?
check.why: Supple means able to bend easily.

lessons.title: The Empty Hub
lessons.mainIdea: Daodejing 11 says the empty space in a wheel's hub, a bowl and a room is what makes them useful.
reading: Chapter 11 gives three pictures. Thirty spokes meet at a wheel's hub. It is the empty space at the center, where the axle goes, that makes the wheel useful.
Next, clay is shaped into a bowl. It is the empty space inside that holds food. Then doors and windows are cut into a room. It is the empty space that makes the room usable.
The chapter ends by saying that what is there gives benefit, but what is not there gives use. Readers see a lesson: emptiness and quiet can matter as much as things.

words.d: the center of a wheel, where the spokes meet
open, empty space; in the Daodejing, what makes things useful

look.title: Daodejing 11
look.text: Thirty spokes meet at one hub. The empty space at its center makes the wheel useful. Clay is shaped into a bowl. The empty space inside makes the bowl useful.
look.cite: Daodejing, chapter 11, retold simply from James Legge's translation (1891)
look.prompt: Name something in your classroom that is useful because of its empty space.

check.q: How many spokes meet at the hub in chapter 11?
check.why: Chapter 11 says thirty spokes.

check.q: What makes a bowl useful, in chapter 11?
check.why: The empty space holds food.

check.q: What is a hub?
check.why: The hub is where the spokes meet.

lessons.title: The Uncarved Block
lessons.mainIdea: The Daodejing uses pu, the uncarved block of wood, as a picture of simplicity before things are shaped or divided.
reading: Another image is *pu*, the uncarved block. Pu is a piece of wood that has not yet been carved into anything. It is plain, whole and full of possibility.
Chapter 19 advises showing plainness and holding on to the uncarved block. Chapter 28 speaks of returning to the uncarved block. The book links it to having fewer wants.
Readers interpret pu in different ways. Some see it as the simple heart a person has before learning to show off. Others see a picture of the Dao itself, before it is divided into many things.

words.d: the uncarved block; plain, whole simplicity in the Daodejing
being plain and not complicated

look.title: Before the Carving
look.text: A woodcarver holds a plain block of wood. It could become a spoon, a bowl, a bird or a box. Once it is carved into a spoon, it can no longer become a bowl. The Daodejing praises the block before carving.
look.prompt: Why might the Daodejing praise the block more than the finished spoon?

check.q: What is pu?
check.why: Pu is the uncarved block of wood.

check.q: What does the uncarved block stand for, in the Daodejing?
check.why: It is a picture of plain, whole simplicity.

check.q: Which chapter speaks of returning to the uncarved block?
check.why: Chapter 28 speaks of returning to pu.

lessons.title: The Small Village
lessons.mainIdea: Daodejing 80 pictures a small, peaceful village whose people are content with a simple life.
reading: Chapter 80 describes a small state with few people. They have tools and boats but seldom use them. They enjoy their food, their clothes and their homes.
The neighboring village is so close that people can hear its roosters and dogs. Yet, the chapter says, people grow old and die without ever visiting it. They are content where they are.
Readers argue about this chapter. Some read it as a picture of peace and contentment. Others see it as an ideal that could never fully work. Some compare it to modern calls to slow down.

words.d: happy with what you have
a picture of how things would be at their best

look.title: A Picture of Chapter 80
look.text: A few houses sit by a river. Smoke rises from cooking fires. Across the field, a rooster crows in the next village. A grandmother hears it, smiles and goes back to her garden. She has never needed to go there.
look.prompt: Would you want to live in this village? What would be good about it, and what would be hard?

check.q: What can people hear from the next village in chapter 80?
check.why: Chapter 80 says they can hear its roosters and dogs.

check.q: What does content mean?
check.why: Content means satisfied with what you have.

check.q: How do readers respond to chapter 80?
choices: All agree it is a map
Some see peace; others see an ideal that could not fully work
check.why: Readers disagree about how to read it.

lessons.title: Knowing When You Have Enough
lessons.mainIdea: The Daodejing teaches that knowing when you have enough brings contentment.
reading: Several chapters talk about wanting less. Chapter 46 says there is no greater trouble than not knowing when you have enough. It says the person who knows enough is always content.
Chapter 44 asks hard questions. Which matters more, your name or your life? Your life or your things? It says knowing when to stop keeps a person from danger.
Many Daoist readers link this to simplicity and the uncarved block. Other traditions have similar teachings. Readers compare them while noticing each tradition's own reasons.

words.d: as much as you need
a calm feeling of being satisfied

look.title: Daodejing 46
look.text: There is no greater trouble than not knowing when you have enough. The one who knows what is enough will always have enough.
look.cite: Daodejing, chapter 46, retold simply from James Legge's translation (1891)
look.prompt: Why might knowing 'enough' be hard for people?

check.q: What does chapter 46 call the greatest trouble?
choices: Not knowing when you have enough
check.why: Chapter 46 says so.

lessons.title: Cook Ding's Knife
lessons.mainIdea: In Zhuangzi 3, Cook Ding's knife stays sharp for 19 years because he follows the natural gaps.
reading: The story of Cook Ding is in chapter 3 of the Zhuangzi. The chapter is often titled 'The Secret of Caring for Life.' Ding cuts an ox so smoothly that it looks like a dance.
Ding says he follows the natural lines and gaps. He does not hack at bone. So his knife stays sharp for 19 years, while other cooks must replace theirs often.
Readers link this story to wu wei. Ding acts with great skill but without forcing. When he reaches a hard spot, he slows down and takes care. The king says he has learned how to care for life.

words.d: the cook in Zhuangzi 3 whose knife stayed sharp by following natural gaps
the ability to do something well, from practice

lessons.title: The Frog in the Well
lessons.mainIdea: In Zhuangzi 17, a frog in a well thinks its small world is everything until a great turtle describes the sea.
reading: Chapter 17 of the Zhuangzi, 'Autumn Floods,' tells of a frog living in a broken-down well. The frog loves its well. It splashes in the water and rests on the edge.
The frog invites a great turtle from the Eastern Sea to come in. But the turtle cannot even fit its leg in. The turtle describes the sea: so huge that floods and droughts barely change it.

The frog is stunned. Readers use this story to talk about limited views. From the bottom of a well, the sky looks small. Today, 'a frog in a well' is a common Chinese saying for someone with a narrow view.

words.d: the way something looks from where you stand
small or limited

look.title: The View from the Well
look.text: The frog looks up from the bottom of the well. It sees a small, round patch of sky. 'That is the whole sky,' it says. The turtle, who has swum the open sea, knows the sky stretches to every horizon.
look.prompt: When have you learned that your view of something was too small?

check.why: A turtle from the Eastern Sea describes it.

check.q: What does 'a frog in a well' mean as a saying?
check.why: It names someone whose view is limited.

lessons.title: Why Teach With Pictures?
lessons.mainIdea: The Daodejing and the Zhuangzi teach with images and stories, which readers can interpret in many ways.
reading: The Analects often gives direct advice about how to act. The Daodejing and Zhuangzi more often give images: water, a hub, a block of wood, a cook, a frog.

An image does not tell you exactly what to think. It asks you to look and wonder. That is one reason these books have so many interpretations. Different readers notice different things in the same picture.
Zhuangzi's stories are also often funny. Scholars note that humor can help people let go of fixed ideas. The images stay in readers' minds long after they finish reading.

what makes something funny
